    Why does March Madness have play-in games?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    Play-in games, known as the
    First Four, were introduced to expand the tournament field to 68 teams while keeping the traditional 64-team first-round bracket intact. These four games allow extra teams (lowest-seeded automatic qualifiers and "last four" at-large teams) to compete for a spot in the main bracket, increasing excitement and revenue. 
    This video explains the excitement and history behind the First Four games:
    58s
    Dagnal Diagonal
    YouTube • Mar 23, 2025
    Key Reasons for the Play-in Games: 
    • Expansion (68 vs. 64): In 2011, the NCAA tournament expanded to 68 teams. The First Four matches decide the last four teams in, creating a clean, traditional 64-team bracket for the first round
      .
    • Preventing Tournament "Snubs": The games allow more deserving schools—both small-conference champions and lower-seeded power conference teams (at-large bids)—to participate, reducing controversies over who was left out, as shown in Wikipedia and this article from SI.com.
    • Increasing "Madness": The games generate early excitement before the main tournament, often allowing lower-seeded, "Cinderella" teams to gain momentum.
    • Historical Context: Beginning in 2001, single play-in games were added to accommodate new conference automatic bids without removing at-large slots, evolving into the First Four format, often held in Dayton, Ohio.
